resetHelp.title: Reset your password
resetHelp.intro: OTW runs on your own server: there is no mailbox to send a reset link to, and no unauthenticated way in. Reset the password from a terminal on the machine that hosts it.
resetHelp.step.shell: Open a shell on the machine running OTW.
resetHelp.step.run: Run this, with your account name in place of USERNAME. It prints a one-time password.
resetHelp.step.signIn: Sign in with that password. The app asks you for a new one straight away.
resetHelp.ownPassword: Rather choose the password yourself? Pipe it in: never pass it as an argument, a process's command line is readable on the host.
resetHelp.renamed: Container named differently? List them and use the core one.
resetHelp.note.sessions: A reset signs out every device.
resetHelp.note.data: Nothing is lost: the vault and stored provider keys are sealed with OTW_SECRET_KEY, not with your password.
resetHelp.note.bare: Not running Docker? Run the otw-core binary with the same arguments and DATABASE_URL set.

settings.network.mode.lanhttpsHint: Reachable on your network over HTTPS with a real certificate: no browser warnings on any device. Nothing is exposed to the internet.
settings.network.lanHttpsHelp: Uses a free Let's Encrypt certificate obtained through your DNS provider (DNS challenge), so it works on a private network without opening any port. DuckDNS is free: sign in at duckdns.org, create a subdomain, and paste its token below.

settings.network.lanIpHint: The DuckDNS record is pointed at this private IP automatically. Correct the prefill if it doesn't match this machine.
settings.network.ctNote: Note: issued certificates are public (Certificate Transparency), so the chosen domain name is publicly visible. The app itself stays LAN-only.
settings.network.err.dnsTokenRequired: A DNS provider token is required.
settings.network.err.lanIpRequired: This machine's LAN IP is required.
settings.network.mode.webHint: Exposed on a domain with automatic HTTPS. Only enable if this host is internet-facing.
settings.network.domainHint: Point this domain’s DNS at this host; Caddy fetches a TLS cert automatically. Served on 443.

settings.backup.selIntro: Download the modules you tick as one file, to move them to another instance or keep a copy you can open. Historical bars start unticked: they are the largest table and can be downloaded again from your provider. For a full safety copy of everything, use the Full tab.
settings.backup.selCredentials: Include stored provider credentials (unreadable on another instance, which has a different encryption key)
settings.backup.selLoadIntro: Load a file downloaded above, from this instance or another one. Everything happens in one step: if anything fails, nothing is changed.
settings.backup.selDropHint: A .zip written by Partial → Backup, on this instance or another one.

settings.backup.selReplace: Replace: erase these modules here, then load the file

settings.backup.title: Backup & restore
settings.backup.intro: Run this on the host where the stack is deployed. It dumps the whole database over the existing Postgres connection: no extra access required.
settings.backup.encryptBody: A dump contains your data in the clear. Pipe it through gpg (or age) so the file is encrypted on disk; you'll be prompted for a passphrase.
settings.backup.security1: API keys/credentials (news feeds, data providers) are already encrypted at rest with OTW_SECRET_KEY, so they appear only as ciphertext in the dump. The backup is useless for those without that key.
settings.backup.security2: Back up OTW_SECRET_KEY (from your .env) separately (not inside the same dump), or encrypted secrets can't be restored.
settings.backup.security3: The dump includes live sessions tokens. Treat the file as a secret, or drop that table after restoring and sign in again.
settings.backup.security4: Store the encrypted backup off-box and rotate older copies.
settings.backup.scheduledDestNone: Kept on this machine only. A copy somewhere else is what survives a dead server.
settings.backup.scheduledVerified: Restore tested: the backup was opened and checked.
settings.backup.scheduledUnverified: Not restore-tested. A backup nobody has restored is not a backup yet.
settings.backup.scheduledStaleHelp: Expected every day. Check the machine is running, then run the backup by hand with the commands below.
settings.update.title: Update app

settings.update.before1: Take a database backup first (see the Backup section).
settings.update.before2: Migrations run automatically on the new container's first boot.
settings.update.before3: Review release notes for any breaking changes.

settings.mcp.note2: Writes require the module’s read+write level; reads require at least read.
settings.mcp.note3: If the app is reachable only on localhost, agents must run on this machine too.

mailbox.setup.gmail: Turn on 2-Step Verification first: Google only offers app passwords once it is on. Paste the 16-character password without its spaces and use your full address as the username. On a Workspace account an admin can have disabled both IMAP and app passwords.
mailbox.setup.icloud: Two-factor authentication is required. Create an app-specific password on account.apple.com (Sign-In and Security → App-Specific Passwords) and sign in with your primary Apple ID address, not an alias.
mailbox.setup.yahoo: Your account password will not work here: generate an app password under Account security → Generate app password (same page for AOL).
mailbox.setup.zoho: Check the server matches your account's region: imap.zoho.eu, .com, .in or .com.au. IMAP has to be enabled in Zoho's mail settings first, and an app password is required when two-factor is on.
mailbox.setup.protonBridge: Proton Mail needs a paid plan and Bridge running on your machine; copy the address, port and Bridge password from Bridge → Settings → IMAP. Bridge's certificate is self-signed and will fail TLS verification, so choose "None": the connection never leaves your machine. And since OpenTraderWorld runs in a container, 127.0.0.1 is the container itself: point the server at the machine running Bridge, which also has to accept a connection from outside its own loopback.

automator.help.title: How the Automator works
automator.help.grid.g1: Steps run top to bottom, and inside a step the tasks run left to right. Everything runs one after another: a step groups the tasks that belong to the same moment of the workflow, it does not start them together.
automator.help.grid.g2: A task can only read what ran before it. Move a card and every reference it makes is checked again on the next save.
automator.help.grid.g3: Drag a block from the panel on the right onto a gap. The gap between two steps opens a new step, the gap between two tasks drops it into that step.
automator.help.grid.g4: The editor saves on its own a moment after each edit, and every change can be undone.
automator.help.data.d1: Each block has an id, shown at the top of its editor. A later block reads its result with {{steps.http1.output}}, and one field of it with {{steps.http1.output.items.0.name}}.
automator.help.data.d2: Readable from anywhere: {{run.started_at}}, {{run.trigger}}, {{workflow.name}}, and {{input.key}} for the values passed to a manual run.
automator.help.data.d3: Filters chain after a pipe: json, upper, lower, trim, round:2, date:"DD/MM/YYYY", default:"n/a". Only default rescues a value that is not there.
automator.help.data.d4: References are checked when the graph is saved, against the blocks that really precede it, so a broken one is refused in the editor instead of at three in the morning.
automator.help.blocks.api: Your app lists the endpoints a workflow may reach, under the blocks on the right. Search it, then click or drag one: it lands already pointed at that call. It runs only with an access token, created in Settings, AI agents, then picked in this workflow's settings.
automator.help.blocks.http: Web call reaches any URL outside the app. An address on your own network or machine is refused unless the block explicitly allows it.
automator.help.blocks.agent: AI step is one model turn, with no conversation around it. Ask for JSON when the block after it has to read fields rather than prose.
automator.help.blocks.transform: Transform reshapes what came before: pick takes one value, set builds an object, format writes a string, csv_parse reads a CSV, join folds a list into one line.
automator.help.blocks.notify: Notify sends to your channels. They are set up once in Settings, Notifications, granted to the Automator there, and only then offered here.
automator.help.blocks.delay: Wait pauses the run. Stop still answers during the wait.
automator.help.secrets.s1: A password or an API key belongs in the vault, never typed into a field. Reference it with {{vault.myvault.mykey}} in a header or a request body, the only two places it is accepted, and the resolved value is kept out of the run history.
automator.help.run.r1: Test run performs the reads and reports what a write or a send would have done, so nothing leaves the app. Run now does it for real.
automator.help.run.r2: A schedule carries its own timezone. If a run is still going when the next occurrence falls due, that occurrence is dropped rather than queued.
automator.help.fail.f1: Each task decides on its own whether to stop the run or carry on, with up to five retries and its own time limit, under Advanced in the block editor.
automator.help.fail.f2: Every run keeps one line per block with what was sent and what came back, so a failure names the block and shows the payload.

settings.risks.title: Trading, third-party and cyber risks
settings.risks.intro: Trading can lose you a lot of money, very quickly. Technology makes analysis and execution faster, but it does not remove uncertainty, model errors, outages, fraud or human mistakes. Read the terms from your broker, data providers and every connected service too.
settings.risks.warning.title: You can lose all of your capital—and sometimes more.
settings.risks.warning.body: Never trade with money needed for rent, daily expenses, emergencies or a near-term bill. With leverage, margin, derivatives, short selling or an illiquid market, you can lose more than you put in.
settings.risks.capital.title: Loss of capital and suitability
settings.risks.capital.p1: A price can move sharply against you and never come back. No stop, model, indicator or diversification rule removes that risk. A product that looks reasonable on screen may still be completely wrong for your situation.
settings.risks.capital.b1: Returns remain uncertain. Your capital, income and purchasing power can all fall.
settings.risks.capital.b2: Positions that look different can drop together. Concentration, correlation and contagion are real.
settings.risks.capital.b3: Currency moves, inflation, rates, fees and tax can turn a headline gain into a real loss.
settings.risks.capital.b4: If you have to sell in a hurry, you may lock in the loss at the worst possible time.
settings.risks.markets.title: Market, liquidity and execution risk
settings.risks.markets.p1: A displayed price is not a promise of execution. When markets race, gap, close or run short of liquidity—or when a connection drops—you may not enter, exit, cancel or hedge in time.
settings.risks.markets.b1: A market order can fill far from the last quote. A limit or stop order may not fill, or may fill at a different price.
settings.risks.markets.b2: Slippage, spreads, commissions, financing, borrow fees and partial fills eat into results. Sometimes heavily.
settings.risks.markets.b3: A short position adds recall and borrow-cost risk. Its theoretical loss is unlimited.
settings.risks.markets.b4: Venue rules, a corporate action, a halt or a settlement failure can block access to your funds or positions.
settings.risks.leverage.title: Leverage, derivatives and digital assets
settings.risks.leverage.p1: Leverage turns a small price move into a large gain or loss. Liquidation can happen in moments. Complex products may also behave very differently from the asset they appear to track.
settings.risks.leverage.b1: A broker can raise margin requirements without warning. You may have to add money or accept a forced sale at a bad price.
settings.risks.leverage.b2: Options, futures, CFDs, perpetuals and leveraged tokens add their own expiry, basis, volatility, funding and counterparty risks.
settings.risks.leverage.b3: Crypto-assets can be highly volatile, thinly traded, manipulated or technically fragile. Legal protection and regulation vary widely.
settings.risks.leverage.b4: Depending on the product and country, you may lose more than your deposit and have no investor compensation scheme to fall back on.
settings.risks.data.title: Market data and calculation risk
settings.risks.data.p1: A result is only as good as its data. Exchange, broker, file and aggregator data can arrive late, be incomplete, duplicated, adjusted badly or simply wrong.
settings.risks.data.b1: One bad time zone, timestamp, symbol, currency, corporate action or contract roll can distort the whole analysis.
settings.risks.data.b2: Missing bars, survivorship bias or a provider's different methodology can change statistics and signals.
settings.risks.data.b3: Derived prices, currency conversions, valuations and tax calculations sometimes rely on estimates or fallback sources.
settings.risks.data.b4: Before acting on something important, confirm it with an independent primary source.
settings.risks.models.title: Backtest, model and optimisation risk
settings.risks.models.p1: A backtest replays the past through a simplified model. That is all. It does not prove a strategy is tradable or profitable, even when the numbers look impressively precise.
settings.risks.models.b1: A smooth historical curve does not predict the next return or the next market regime.
settings.risks.models.b2: Look-ahead, selection, survivorship and data-snooping bias can manufacture an edge that is not real.
settings.risks.models.b3: Optimise and retest often enough and you can fit the strategy to noise. Even an out-of-sample period loses value once you reuse it.
settings.risks.models.b4: Fees, slippage, latency, liquidity, rejections, market impact and tax are simplified, estimated or missing.
settings.risks.models.b5: VaR, correlations, volatility, Kelly sizing and stress tests all rely on assumptions. In a crisis, those assumptions are often the first things to break.
settings.risks.automation.title: Automation and artificial intelligence
settings.risks.automation.p1: An automation or AI system can misunderstand the request, invent a fact, choose the wrong tool, repeat an action or keep going after conditions change. The answer may sound certain and still be completely wrong.
settings.risks.automation.b1: Treat every AI answer as unverified. Check important facts and actions somewhere else.
settings.risks.automation.b2: A prompt, document, web page or external tool may contain malicious instructions designed to redirect the agent.
settings.risks.automation.b3: A retry, bad time zone or duplicate event can skip a workflow—or run it twice.
settings.risks.automation.b4: With a valid token, an agent can read, change or delete everything its permissions allow.
settings.risks.automation.b5: Put human approval, strict limits and an independent kill switch in front of every financial or irreversible action.
settings.risks.thirdparty.title: Third-party services and counterparties
settings.risks.thirdparty.p1: Your broker, exchange, bank, data or AI vendor, mail server and messaging service do not belong to OpenTraderWorld. The publisher controls none of their security, solvency, accuracy or availability.
settings.risks.thirdparty.b1: An API can change its rules, throttle requests, suspend an account, return bad data or shut down without warning.
settings.risks.thirdparty.b2: A provider can reject, delay, repeat or mishandle a request or transaction.
settings.risks.thirdparty.b3: Once sent, your data and credentials are governed by the provider's security, retention and privacy rules.
settings.risks.thirdparty.b4: Fraud, insolvency, counterparty default or custody failure can make assets inaccessible, sometimes permanently.
settings.risks.thirdparty.b5: Read the permissions, fees, licences and terms. Keep a direct recovery route for every account too.
settings.risks.cyber.title: Cybersecurity and self-hosting risk
settings.risks.cyber.p1: Self-hosting keeps you in control. It also makes you the system administrator. AI-assisted security audits are run at regular intervals, but they are still point-in-time checks. They do not replace an independent audit, penetration test or certification, and they can miss a vulnerability. The security of the host, the instance and the data stored on it is never guaranteed.
settings.risks.cyber.b1: Expose the instance to the internet or LAN and you invite scans, password attacks, exploit attempts and unauthorised access.
settings.risks.cyber.b2: If the host, an extension, a dependency or the update chain is compromised, application controls may be bypassed.
settings.risks.cyber.b3: A stolen session, API key, MCP token, backup or environment file can open access to data and connected services.
settings.risks.cyber.b4: Hardware failure, ransomware, deletion, database corruption or a bad update can cause permanent loss when no working backup exists.
settings.risks.cyber.b5: Encryption at rest protects the disk, not data that is already open, in use, exported, logged or sent through an authorised integration.
settings.risks.privacy.title: Privacy and data flows
settings.risks.privacy.p1: On a self-hosted installation, data stays on infrastructure you control. There is no publisher telemetry and no central OpenTraderWorld account. Your journal, portfolios, keys, prompts and other private records are not sent automatically to the publisher or author.
settings.risks.privacy.p2: Data leaves only when you use a feature that contacts something outside the instance: a market or broker API, AI provider, feed, email or messaging service, webhook, MCP server, community sync or ordinary link. That service receives what it needs to answer, which may include an identifier, content or network metadata. Its own rules then apply.
settings.risks.privacy.p3: A publisher-operated service sees the normal technical metadata of a connection. Beyond that, the publisher receives only what you choose to send: a contribution, support request, security report or issue, for example. Review it first and remove secrets and personal data.
settings.risks.privacy.b1: No publisher telemetry does not mean no outbound connections or no logs held by third parties.
settings.risks.privacy.b2: Your host, reverse proxy, DNS provider, network operator and connected services may retain metadata or content.
settings.risks.privacy.b3: Depending on your deployment and access rules, another user or administrator of the instance may be able to see the data.
settings.risks.privacy.b4: You handle the notice, consent, retention, deletion and cross-border transfer duties that apply to the data you process.
settings.risks.demo.title: Public demonstration environment
settings.risks.demo.p1: The public demo is shared. It is not private. Other visitors may see what you enter, and everything is erased regularly. Never put real personal, financial, confidential or credential data there.
settings.risks.demo.p2: The demo has less data, AI capacity and availability than a local installation. Do not use it to make decisions, keep information, test a backup or assess security.
settings.risks.controls.title: Minimum precautions
settings.risks.controls.p1: You cannot remove risk. A few simple habits can still prevent a lot of avoidable damage.
settings.risks.controls.b1: Keep the instance local when you can. If you expose it, use HTTPS, a firewall and a trusted reverse proxy.
settings.risks.controls.b2: Choose strong, unique passwords. Turn on two-factor authentication and give tokens as little access and lifetime as possible.
settings.risks.controls.b3: Patch the host and application promptly, but read the release notes first.
settings.risks.controls.b4: Keep encrypted backups offline or off-site. Test a full restore regularly.
settings.risks.controls.b5: Watch logs, sessions, provider activity and account statements. Revoke anything you do not recognise immediately.
settings.risks.controls.b6: Start in sandbox or paper mode. Set conservative limits, check results elsewhere and keep manual control.
